answers.text: Lock the output to three fixed lines in a set order so it can't drift between runs. Define each line exactly — time only, pallet count alone, damage or 'none' — no overlap between lines. If any field is missing, say to write 'not stated', never leave it blank or invent a figure.

Fix the output shape up front — one row per call, set field order, a clear follow-up marker. State that the follow-up count is derived by summing the flagged entries, not asserted separately. Say explicitly what to do with a duplicate-looking entry — flag it, don't silently merge or drop it.

The timing in this note doesn't reconcile with itself. The six-hour estimate from an 8am start resolves same-day, so the note's finish date doesn't follow. It comes down to the finish date disagreeing with its own arithmetic — six hours doesn't reach the next day.
Recalculating, 96 to 118 comes out at about 23%, not the stated 20%. The on-time rate itself is consistent: 9 late out of 118 is roughly 92%, matching what's stated.

I'd sign off Output 2 — it shows the source figures and the calculation. What's missing from Output 1 is the 940 and the 827 themselves. Output 1's figure isn't necessarily wrong, only unconfirmable without an independent re-count.

I'd send Email 2 without further checking — it cites the volume figures and PO log. The claim in Email 1 that can't be checked is the rate expectation itself; nothing supports it. I wouldn't reject Email 1 outright; add the PO log figures and it becomes equally sendable.

1. No.

The rate figures get redacted or held back until the tool itself is vetted. Because the NDA clause names both the client and us, it gets the same caution as the pricing. The general scope of service carries little risk and can go in unredacted.

I'd add a named cross-cast step: recompute the month's stock totals independently and compare. That check sits right before the reconciliation reaches finance, not earlier in the process. Because it's a genuine cross-cast against the warehouse system, it would catch a wrong total or fabricated line.

An error at extraction doesn't stay contained; it propagates through the PO match and approval note. Step 4 is where an error becomes irreversible — once it auto-submits, there's no catching it after. The gate should flag an invoice with unusually large extracted totals, or a PO match right at the boundary.
